name: io.github.Mvp2o-ai/cuttingfloor
title: cuttingfloor
description: Hosted video editing for AI agents: cut, caption, mix and export real video. Sign in with OAuth.

tools.name: timeline.create
tools.description: Start an empty timeline. Returns its timeline_id and its tracks (ids for track_id). Where no clip covers the picture it is black (transparent in a nested timeline). Timelines are immutable: every edit returns a new timeline_id, and older ids stay valid for 7 days after last use. For work longer than that, keep the timeline.get document on your side and restore it with timeline.load.

tracks.description: How many empty tracks to start with

tools.name: timeline.get
tools.description: The full timeline: tracks, clips (frames, end exclusive), link groups and the media it uses. The server keeps a timeline 7 days after last use: for work longer than that, save this document on your side (it is the edit) and restore it with timeline.load.

timeline_id.description: Timeline handle; every edit returns a new one

tools.name: timeline.load
tools.description: Restore a timeline from the document timeline.get returned, e.g. after it expired (7 days after last use). Its media must still be here: media expires 7 days after last use, so import saved files again with media.import and swap them in with clip.replace.

tools.name: audio.set_gain
tools.description: Volume of an audio clip (or a video clip's linked audio) in dB; keyframes ride it up and down. The preview is a waveform of the clip; with preview inline it also carries the measured loudness (preview.loudness), a link preview does not. Returns the new timeline_id (edit that one next), what changed, and where each changed clip now sits.

Keyframes make a ride: the first key holds backward to the clip start, so a ride that begins part-way down must also key its starting level at frame 0 or the frames before it are changed too. A key past the clip end is stored as given, with no clamp and no warning. Two keys on one frame are refused

tools.name: filter.add

Order matters: effects run in the order added (a track's before a clip's own). Picture numbers take keyframes, except glitch, denoise and chroma_key tolerance; sound params are constants. tools.name: media.analyze
tools.description:
Find what is in imported media, or in the sound of an edit, as data for edits. transcript: every word with its time (whisper.cpp on the CPU; the model downloads once). For English the word edges are then aligned to the sound (wav2vec2 forced alignment): a word starts and ends within about 0.05 s of where its letters sound, and an end on a soft consonant (s, t, k, f) or a breath can ring on up to about 0.1 s more; timing_confidence says how clearly each word was heard. Other languages keep whisper's own times, up to about a second off. Short ums and uhs are often missing from the words, while kind speech still detects them as voice. from_seconds and until_seconds transcribe just that stretch: the words come back in the result and are not stored, so the stored transcript (which edits and captions read) stays the whole media's. file: txt also writes the transcript as a file on the cutting floor, with a download url. beats: tempo, beat and downbeat times, and strengths: each beat's onset strength, 0–1 of the strongest (the hardest hits, the drop). faces: face boxes over time, e.g. to reframe to 9:16 with clip.set_transform keyframes. track: follow a region you give from a moment on, a box for each sampled time (found false where the subject was lost); to make a title, sticker, arrow or mask follow the subject, turn the boxes into clip.set_transform (or clip.set_mask) keyframes, no tracking of your own needed. look: your own typed questions about what is on screen, answered on every sampled frame (to find where something happens from plain words, media.seek). silence: stretches quieter than threshold_db for at least min_seconds. scenes: times the picture changes by more than threshold (0–100; hard cuts between ordinary shots score about 10 to 30, see threshold), with each cut's score. speech: the probability that someone is speaking, every 32 ms (Silero VAD), and the spans where it is at least your min_probability; it hears speech, not noise or music, so a cough or a door is not speech. loudness: integrated loudness (LUFS), true peak (dBTP), loudness range (LU), RMS level and noise floor (dBFS) over the whole media or from_seconds to until_seconds. To line up two recordings, media.correlate. sounds: what can be heard and when, every 40 ms, for 447 named sounds (video://catalog/sounds: Laughter, Applause, Cough, Sneeze, Music, Speech, Door, Footsteps, Beep…): give labels for the ones you want, or none for every sound that reaches your min_probability; you get each sound's spans and its probability in every frame (a run over the whole media is kept with it; one over from_seconds to until_seconds comes back only). To find a sound you describe in your own words, media.listen. Both find sounds in the media; sound effects to add come from sounds.list. speakers: who speaks when (pyannote and ERes2Net on the CPU, about 10 to 20 s a minute): turns numbered in the order voices are first heard; give speakers (how many) or cluster_threshold. Transcript words then carry their speaker. voice: pitch (YIN, Hz) and level (RMS dBFS) every 0.1 s, and a summary (pitch median and range, level, voiced seconds, words per second from the transcript), e.g. as judge.ask state. colour: per-channel mean and percentiles, luma, white point estimate and clipping (RGB 0–255) of the frame and regions you name, at sampled times. picture: FFmpeg signalstats of every frame over a stretch: luma, chroma, saturation, hue, and ydif, the change from the frame before (a flash or frozen frame shows there).
With timeline_id instead of media_id, speech, loudness, silence, sounds, speakers, voice measure the edit's mix and faces, track, look, scenes, colour, picture its picture as it renders (titles, effects and grades included), over from_seconds to until_seconds (timeline seconds); they come back in the result. A source or range with no sound fails with no_audio, naming it.
Times are media seconds (timeline seconds for a timeline); boxes are fractions of the picture, and a box you give takes units "pixels" too (picture_size gives the size). Results stay with the media (media.get include; the latest run of each kind) except track, silence, scenes and loudness, which come back in the result; speech over the whole media is kept (media.get include speech), so asking again with another min_probability or range answers from it. A result too long to return (a long transcript) comes back as its summary and a note: read it in pieces with media.get include and a time range or page.
Long-running: returns a task, or a job_id for job.get.

HOW LOOK WORKS. A fast judgment model (preview) answers your questions about frames sampled from the media. Each sampled frame is its own request: the judgment model sees that one picture, named `frame`, and with with_previous also the frame sampled just before it, named `previous`, plus any state you give: text or JSON entries by name, the same on every frame (the script, what a term means). Every question is answered on every frame, independently and in parallel (about 0.15 s a frame), as typed data you then combine in your own code.
Choose the type by the answer you need. noul: yes or no, answered as noul, the probability of yes from 0 to 1. choice: one of options you name, answered as choice plus probabilities and confidence. score: a degree on levels you order, answered as score (0 is the first level; it can land between levels) plus confidence. box: where one thing is, answered as box {x, y, w, h} in fractions of the picture plus confidence.
Write each question about the picture as it looks. Name the picture in backticks ("in `frame`"), ask about one thing, word it so yes means the thing is there, and describe it as it appears: "Does `frame` show a human being, even if only their face fills the picture?", "Is one large word laid over `frame`, much bigger than any other text?". To compare, name both pictures and the thing that differs: "Is there a button in `frame` that is not in `previous`?". To locate, name the one thing so only it fits ("the 'Get started for free' button under the headline in `frame`") and, in the same call, a noul asking whether it is there; use the box on frames where that noul is high. Give a choice a none option for frames where nothing fits, and each score level a concrete situation.
Read the answers this way: a noul of 0.5 or more reads as yes, and you can set your own cut-off; confidence tells you how far to trust a choice, a score or a box, and a loose box shows as low confidence. Work in passes: every_seconds 1 over the whole media, then at_seconds around the times where answers change. media.get scenes give when the picture cuts; look tells you what is on it.
The result gives each question's spans (when a noul reads yes, which choice holds when); every frame's answers stay with the media (media.get include ['look'], the last 10 runs). Up to 600 frames and 32 questions a call. To find the moments that match a description, media.seek takes it in plain words and returns where it holds. For one judgment about text, a still or a single frame, judge.ask answers at once. Full guide to writing questions: https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives and https://docs.typesafe.ai/images.

tools.name: media.correlate
tools.description:
Find how far one recording sits from another: the sync offset of b against a, by cross-correlating their sound, with how strongly they match. Use it to line up a camera with a separate microphone, two cameras of the same moment, or a re-recorded line against the original. Each side is imported media or an edit's mix (timeline_id), over its own from_seconds to until_seconds, so you can match a short stretch of b against a longer stretch of a.
offset_seconds: b's moment t lines up with a's moment t + offset_seconds, each in its own seconds. To line them up on a timeline, place b's clip so it starts offset_seconds later than a's (earlier when negative), source starts being equal. strength is the correlation of the overlapping sound at that offset, -1 to 1: near 1 the same sound, near 0 unrelated; next_best is the best offset outside the winning peak, and a strength close to it means the match is unclear (repetitive sound, or not the same moment). Offsets are searched up to max_offset_seconds either way, where at least half of the shorter sound overlaps the other. Up to 600 s read from each side.
A side with no sound in its range (no audio stream, a range past its end, or digital silence) fails with no_audio, naming which side. Short reads answer at once; longer ones return a task or job.

tools.name: media.seek
tools.description:
Find the moments in a video, or in an edit as it renders, that match what you describe in plain words, so you go straight to them instead of watching it all. Name each criterion and say what a matching frame shows; you get back the stretches of time where each one holds, with the time and picture of the best frame in each.
Use it to:
- Check quality: find frames that are too dark or blown out, out of focus, black or blank (a gap in an edit), with a microphone or crew in shot, with text cut off at the edge, or with a caption over a face. With timeline_id it checks the edit as it renders, titles, effects and gaps included.
- Watch efficiently: looking through a whole video costs you a picture for every moment. Seek judges the frames for you and says where things are, so you look only there: where the demo starts, where the speaker holds up the product, where the second location begins.
- Pick shots: B-roll or a thumbnail moment that fits a description ("a wide shot of a city street at night", "she smiles straight at the camera with her eyes open").
- Find changes: with with_previous, where the slide changes, someone walks in or the camera angle switches ("`frame` shows a different slide from `previous`").
- Find room or trouble for overlays: where the lower third stays empty for a title, or where a logo, a licence plate or a face appears that needs a blur.

HOW TO WRITE CRITERIA. A fast judgment model (preview) judges each sampled frame on its own, as a picture named `frame` (about 512 px on its long edge; with with_previous also `previous`, the frame sampled before), and gives each criterion the probability that it is true. A criterion is a statement or a question about how the picture looks. Keep one judgment to a criterion, and say what shows rather than a verdict: not "bad lighting" but "the faces are too dark to make out their eyes"; not "a good thumbnail" but "a person looks straight at the camera with eyes open and mouth closed". Criteria that name no picture or state entry in backticks are asked about `frame` ("In `frame`: <your words>"); name `frame`, `previous` or your state entries yourself to judge them together ("`frame` shows the button `line` talks about"). The judgment model answers most accurately from examples: give {instructions, criteria: {true: "…", false: "…"}} with a case of each ({true: "the face is a dark silhouette against a bright window", false: "the face is evenly lit, a little dim"}). Detail too small to see at that size (fine print, slight softness) answers poorly; check it with render.frames at full size.
READING THE RESULT. matches gives, per criterion, each run of consecutive samples at or above min_probability (default 0.5), with its start, end and best sample: peak_seconds, frame (for render.frames) and uri (a resource to read the picture). samples has every probability, for your own cut-off. A probability near 0.5 means the judgment model cannot tell, not that the thing is half there: reword a criterion that keeps landing there. asked shows the question each criterion became.
COST. Each frame is one judgment however many criteria it carries, so ask everything you are looking for in one call (up to 32 criteria). Work in passes: every_seconds 2 to 5 over the whole video, then at_seconds around a match to find more exactly where it starts. Sampling sees only the frames it samples, so no match can't prove a one-frame defect (a flash, a black or dropped frame) absent: read every frame of a suspect stretch with render.frames, or measure black frames with qa.check. Up to 600 frames a call. Long-running: returns a task, or a job_id for job.get.
media.analyze look asks typed questions (a choice, a score, a box) of every frame when you need measurements rather than moments; judge.ask judges one picture at once.

tools.name: media.search
tools.description:
Find moments across all the user's media from what you describe in plain words: media.seek across every file instead of one. looks criteria are judged on pictures: each keyframe of every video (a new keyframe wherever the picture changes, at least every 10 s, picked when the media was indexed) and each image. says criteria are judged on ~30 s passages of transcripts the media already has. You get matches per criterion across files (media, start, end, best moment and its picture), most probable first.
SIZE. Each keyframe or passage judged is one judgment, however many criteria (up to 32) it carries; searching spends no credits, but judgments take time. Images take 1 each; a 10-minute video about 50 to 260 by how much its picture changes. Every file the search keeps adds to it, so narrow first: kind, media_ids, from, name_contains, duration and from/until_seconds cut what is judged before anything is. candidates keeps the N media whose pictures look most like looks by local similarity, far quicker, though it can drop media where the thing is small or brief. Ask everything you are looking for in one call.
A search estimated over 200 judgments is not run: the result has searched false, the estimate (judgments, by kind, the largest media) and what the filters could cut. Tell the user how big it is and run it again with cost_override once they agree.
HOW TO WRITE CRITERIA. As for media.seek: say what a matching picture shows or what the speech says, one judgment each, with {instructions, criteria: {true, false}} examples for accuracy. Pictures are judged at about 512 px, so small detail (a logo in a corner, fine print) can be missed.
skipped lists media the filters kept that were not judged, and why (still indexing after import, no transcript, outside candidates): not found there is not the same as not there. Long-running: returns a task, or a job_id for job.get.

tools.name: media.listen
tools.description:
Find when something can be heard in a video or audio file, or in an edit as it plays, from what you describe in plain words, so you go straight to it instead of listening to it all: laughter, applause, a cough, a door slamming, a phone ringing, a dog barking, music starting, someone typing, a car passing. Name each sound and say what it is; you get back the stretches of time where each one can be heard, with the moment it is clearest. Sound effects to add to an edit come from sounds.list.
Use it to:
- Find reactions and moments: where the crew or the audience laughs, where people clap or cheer, a gasp, a scream.
- Find trouble to cut or cover: a cough, a sneeze, a phone going off, a door, a siren, wind on the microphone, a click or a bump.
- Find sound to cut on: a clap, a bang, a hit, the music starting or stopping.

HOW IT WORKS. FlexSED, an open-vocabulary sound detection model (local, on the CPU; about 15 to 20 times faster than real time), listens to every 40 ms of the sound and gives each description the probability that it can be heard there. Describe the sound itself, briefly, as you would caption it ("laughter", "a crowd cheering", "glass breaking"), not the scene or a judgment; it is asked as "The sound of <your words>". Short, common sound names work best; put each sound you want in its own entry, up to 16 a call, all listened for at once.
LIMITS. Inside music it hears "music", not drums, instruments or single hits (for hits in music, media.analyze beats). Inside speech it hears "speech", not what is said: words and fillers such as um sound alike to it. A short sound can score higher over a short from_seconds to until_seconds around it.
READING THE RESULT. matches gives, per sound, each run of frames at or above min_probability (default 0.5) with its start, end, peak_seconds and frame (for render.frames; media frames for video, timeline frames for an edit). peaks gives the highest probability each sound reaches, and scores every probability (step_seconds apart), for your own cut-off. A sound whose peak stays well under your cut-off is most likely not there; one hovering near it is worth a listen or a lower cut-off.
Media or an edit: with media_id, times are the file's own seconds; with timeline_id, it listens to the edit's mix as it plays (cuts, gaps, levels and effects included), over from_seconds to until_seconds, and times are timeline seconds, so a match is where that sound now sits in the edit. A source or range with no sound fails with no_audio, naming it.
For the 447 sounds with names (Laughter, Applause, Cough, Speech, Music…) as stored data, media.analyze kind sounds. Long-running: returns a task, or a job_id for job.get.

tools.name: judge.ask
tools.description:
Answer your questions about text and pictures you give (yes or no, a choice, a score, or where something is in a picture), as typed answers in about a second. It asks a fast judgment model (preview).
The judgment model sees exactly the state: each entry under its name, and your questions refer to entries by name in backticks ("in `passage`"). An entry is text (a string, or a JSON object or array of related facts) or a picture: {media_id} for an imported image, {media_id, at_seconds} for the frame of a video at that time, {timeline_id, at_seconds} for a frame of an edit as it renders (to judge a grade or a layout you made). Mix them freely. Each call stands alone, so put everything a judgment needs into its state.
Choose the type by the answer you need. noul: yes or no, answered as noul, the probability of yes from 0 to 1 (0.5 or more reads as yes). choice: one of options you name, answered as choice plus probabilities and confidence. score: a degree on levels you order, answered as score (0 is the first level) plus confidence. box: where one thing is in a picture, answered as box {x, y, w, h} in fractions of that picture plus confidence.
Write each question as one thing, worded so yes means it is there. Open with what the state is ("`passage` is a transcript of someone speaking off the cuff"), and give a noul criteria {true, false} with an example of each: the judgment model answers most accurately from examples. To locate, name the one thing so only it fits ("the yellow headline 'Get started' at the top of `shot`") and ask a noul whether it is there; trust a box with high confidence.
One call answers many questions about one state at once, so judge many items together: put the shared text in state once, and give each item its own question carrying its own watermarked copy. Filler words: state {passage: "So basically the way this works is"}, and per word a noul "`passage` is a transcript of someone speaking off the cuff. With one word marked: "So [[basically]] the way this works is". Is the marked word filler, so the sentence says the same without it?" with criteria {true: "the [[the]] report is late", false: "the report is [[late]]"}. A shot: state {shot: {media_id, at_seconds: 12.5}}, choice "What fills `shot`?" with options {speaker: "A person talking to camera", screen: "A screen recording", none: "Anything else"}. Both: state {line: "Click Get started", screen: {media_id, at_seconds: 4}}, noul "Does `screen` show the button `line` talks about?".
Up to 300 questions, 8 pictures and 200k characters of text a call. To find where something shows in a video or an edit, media.seek takes it in plain words; to measure every frame, media.analyze look asks your questions of frames it samples. Guide to writing questions: https://docs.typesafe.ai/primitives and https://docs.typesafe.ai/images.

Demucs v4 (htdemucs), local, on the CPU: about a fifth of the media's length on 8 cores (a minute of sound in about 15 s). Built for music; on speech with background noise, vocals keeps the voice and other takes most of the noise. Media up to 3 hours. tools.description: Make a person on camera say different words: their mouth is redrawn to match the speech you give (a re-recorded line, a create.voiceover, a word taken from elsewhere in the take). Runs at the user's lip-sync provider on their own key (sync. labs), and the provider bills them for each second sent. Only for the user's own footage, or people who agreed to it (cuttingfloor.ai/acceptable-use). To replace a line or swap a word, give range, the span of the video where it is said, and audio (with audio_range) holding just the new words. The result is that span alone, re-synced and carrying the new speech, as long as the speech with sync_mode remap; place it over the original span (clip.add on a track above, or clip.replace) and mute the old words. Send only the span: it costs less and finishes sooner. Lip sync is for when the face stays on screen while the words change. When the speaker is off screen at that moment, or a cutaway (b-roll, the screen being talked about, a reaction) can cover the splice, the cutaway hides the edit without it. Takes minutes. Long-running: a task, or {job_id, media_id} for job.get. The same recipe returns the same media. Provider limits (plan length, credits, file size) come back as limit_exceeded with the provider's error_code.

tools.description: Measure the rendered timeline: gaps in the picture, offline media, rendered against expected frame count, integrated loudness (LUFS) and true peak (dBTP), plus black and silent stretches when you give their settings. With speech {min_probability}, every cut is listed with speech facts: the speech probability of the mix just before and after it (Silero VAD), the seconds without speech each side, and, per clip edge, the transcript word it cuts through and how much of that word is lost (from the media's transcript, when it has one). Facts only, no verdicts. A timeline up to 20 s is checked within the call (which waits its turn for a render when the server is busy) and answers as a completed job, the report in result; longer ones return a task or job.

timeline_id.description: Timeline handle; every edit returns a new one

black.description: Find black stretches with these settings; left out, none are looked for

pixel_threshold.description: A pixel this dark or darker is black

picture_share.description: A frame with this share of black pixels is black

silence.description: Find silent stretches in the mix with these settings; left out, none are looked for

speech.description: List every cut with speech facts (Silero VAD on the mix, and the transcript word each clip edge cuts through); left out, cuts are not listed. Only junctions between two clips are listed, so a lone clip reports none and its own head and tail are never examined. A null word means the edge falls between words: that is a clean cut, not a missing reading

min_probability.description: A 32 ms frame of the mix with at least this speech probability is speech

tools.name: export.release
tools.description: Removes the watermark from a finished file that has a cuttingfloor watermark (watermarked: true on its export result, media.get or media.list), spending its release_credits (priced by length) once from the user's credits. Afterwards every link to it (url, page_url, media.get) serves the clean file, and this returns fresh ones. Tell the user the price and get their go-ahead first. Releasing again, or a file that never had the watermark, spends nothing. Not enough credits: quota_exceeded, and the watermarked file still downloads.

job_id.description: An export.video job, or the create.* job that made a media

media_id.description: A media made by an export, a create.* tool or a still: removes the watermark from its own file

tools.name: job.get
tools.description: Status, progress and, once completed, the result of long-running calls (media.import, media.analyze, create.*, export.video, qa.check). Same record as tasks/get. status_message says what it is doing, or where it stands in the queue; for names the media or timeline. wait_seconds (up to 50) answers when any job asked for finishes, fails or is cancelled, or when the wait runs out (then with its progress), so one call waits instead of many polls. seconds_left and starts_in_seconds come only when progress so far allows. job_ids reads many and answers {jobs, not_found}, each result in brief (result_summary: lists cut to their first items, with what was cut) unless result is full; result summary does the same for one job. A job whose progress stops for minutes ends with a stalled error, freeing its slot.

job_id.description: One job: the answer is that job

job_ids.description: Many jobs at once (up to 100): the answer is {jobs, not_found}

items.description: Job handle; the same value is the MCP task id

wait_seconds.description: Wait up to this long (at most 50 s) for any job asked for to finish (its status changes); progress along the way does not end the wait; 0 answers at once

result.description: Default full for one job_id; summary for job_ids, so a check on many stays small (full gives them whole)

tools.name: job.list
tools.description: Your recent jobs, newest first, each with its status, progress and for (the media or timeline it is for), filtered by status, tool or media_id. Results are left out unless you ask (result summary or full); job.get reads one.

tool.description: Only jobs of this tool, e.g. media.import

media_id.description: Only jobs for this media (importing, making or reading it)

result.description: none (default): each job without its result, to find one; summary: lists cut short; full: every result whole

tools.name: job.cancel
tools.description: Stop a job, queued or running, within seconds: its engines are killed and its slot goes to the next job. Finished jobs are left as they are.

job_id.description: Job handle; the same value is the MCP task id

tools.name: export.timeline
tools.description: Write the edit for another editor: fcpxml (Final Cut Pro, DaVinci Resolve), otio (Premiere, Resolve, OpenTimelineIO apps), edl (CMX 3600, one video track), or srt/vtt (the captions). Best effort: warnings lists what the format could not carry (masks, blend modes, effects, animated transforms, ramps, text styling). timeline.get is the lossless copy. media reference (default) points at the media where this server keeps it, which another machine cannot open and which goes 7 days after last use (the result warns); media collect makes a .zip with the media files next to the timeline file, to hand the edit on. Long-running: a task, or {job_id} for job.get; the result has a signed download URL.

timeline_id.description: Timeline handle; every edit returns a new one

format.description: fcpxml: Final Cut Pro, Resolve; otio: Premiere, Resolve, any OTIO app; edl: CMX 3600; srt/vtt: captions

media.description: reference: point at the media where it is; collect: a .zip with the media in it

filename.description: Output file name without extension. Default: timeline name and id

tools.name: skills.search
tools.description: Find step-by-step instructions for a common job, written for you to follow with these tools: cutting the pauses, ums and restarts out of a talking video, for one. Search in the user's words: the skills that fit come back, best first. When none fits, or with no query, the answer is the list of every skill, a page at a time, to choose from by description. Read one with skills.get, then follow its Steps.

query.description: What the user wants done, in their words, e.g. "remove the ums from my video". Without it, the list of every skill

offset.description: Where a page of the list starts: the next_offset of the page before

tools.name: skills.get
tools.description: The whole skill as Markdown: when to use it, what it needs, numbered Steps naming the tools to call, a decision table and the rules to keep. Follow the Steps in order.

tools.name: credits.claim
tools.description: Activate the user's cuttingfloor account with the task they want to do, in their words. Personalises their start: records what they're making, adds a sample video that fits it to their library (playing here) and returns their balance. Once per account; later calls return the balance.

use_case.description: What task the user is looking to complete with cuttingfloor, in their words where possible

tools.name: support.contact
tools.description: Send a message to the cuttingfloor team: something failing or erroring; cuttingfloor not being able to do what the user asked; the user asking for a new feature or improvement; or a use case or capability the product does not yet handle - anything that would have helped the user or you be more successful. Filing it is useful even when nothing is broken. Returns an acknowledgement.

message.description: What the user was trying to do, and what happened or could not happen
